sources.title: Seton Lloyd and James Mellaart, Beycesultan II: Middle Bronze Age Architecture and Pottery (1965)
sources.note: Original BIAA monograph publisher description and chapter extracts checked. Arzawa association is tentative, not a demonstrated ancient name.

sources.title: British Institute at Ankara, Beycesultan excavation archive
sources.note: Institutional archive description directly checked: six seasons 1954-1959, Bronze Age city and subsequent occupation. Used for discovery and continued settlement, not precise dynasty identification.

sources.title: Çiğdem Maner and colleagues, Untwisting Beycesultan Höyük (2025)
sources.note: Full original paper directly read. Discovery of textile fragments, fibre results and conclusions. Tx1 context 1915-1745 BCE; hemp/looping and local woad interpretations qualified. Room 28 1700-1595 BCE. No secure ancient site name.

sources.title: Gürkan Ergün, Late Bronze Age spindle whorls and loom weights from Beycesultan (2020)
sources.note: Original eighteen-page PDF directly read. DOI 10.5281/zenodo.3746938. Printed pp. 1-3, 6-7 and household conclusions; updated radiocarbon chronology differs from old excavation dating.

sources.title: Benjamin S. Arbuckle, Pastoralism, Provisioning, and Power at Bronze Age Acemhöyük, Turkey (2012)
sources.note: Original publisher indexed abstract checked; direct publisher request 403. Uses its explicit argument for provisioning, wool markets and pastoral autonomy, no invented species counts or menu.

sources.title: Nimet Özgüç, An Ivory Box and a Stone Mould from Acemhöyük (1976)
sources.note: Original excavation article full text directly checked, pp. 555-560. Box Ac. 0:24 context level III; mould Ac. 1:85 and interpretation that unfinished design ran out of space.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Furniture element with a monkey, 36.152.8a,b
sources.note: Direct original museum record checked. Eighteenth century BCE, hippopotamus ivory, probably from Acemhöyük. Probable provenance retained.

sources.title: Türkiye UNESCO tentative-list submission, Archaeological Site of Kültepe-Kanesh (2014)
sources.note: Full official nomination description directly checked. Tentative list, not an inscribed World Heritage property. Houses, drainage, private archives and local rulers. Kanesh is outside this imported polygon and publicly identified as comparative context.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Cuneiform tablet: private letter, 66.245.1
sources.note: Direct original museum description checked. Old Assyrian twentieth-nineteenth century BCE, probably Kanesh; Imdi-ilum firm, Puzur-Ashur and detained companions. No claim that local residents were all Assyrian.

sources.title: CNRS, Live from Mesopotamia, 4,000 years ago (2026), interview with Cécile Michel
sources.note: Direct institutional research interview read. Different levels of writing and merchant-family sections. Uses attributed teaching interpretation, not claim of universal literacy or a school at Beycesultan.

sources.title: Cécile Michel and colleagues, Kt 94/k 1150, University of Hamburg research dataset (2025)
sources.note: Direct scholarly dataset read. Excavated Kanesh tablet in Ankara museum, Old Assyrian c. 1920-1850 BCE; transliteration lines 1-2 and supplied English translation. X-ray tomography reads enveloped tablet. This is a neighboring community witness, not the language of all mapped communities.

proposedOverrides.name: Anatolian tribes
proposedOverrides.summary: Diverse Bronze Age Anatolian cities, households and regional networks; a broad map category rather than one tribe or state.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: One new regional archaeological overview, no aliases.
batchIdentityNotes.geometry: One decoded Polygon from hb/borders/world-bc2000.json, bbox [26.06447,35.97145,38.90600,40.71057]. Point-in-polygon tests put Beycesultan, Acemhöyük and Troy inside, Kanesh and Hattusha outside. Public opening and each neighboring section preserve this distinction.
batchIdentityNotes.boundaries: The imported label is not an attested collective ethnic or political name. No Hittite/Luwian/Phrygian/Lydian identity merger. No attribution of Beycesultan to Arzawa as established fact. No Hittite imperial institutions or Iron Age practices projected backward.
batchIdentityNotes.writing: No common language follows from the atlas label. The secure contemporary Old Assyrian witness is explicitly from neighboring Kanesh outside the polygon, not passed off as native language of the entire mapped area.
batchIdentityNotes.chronology: Old palace chronology differs from revised late-household phases. Passages use context-specific published dates, with no invented exact point-year metadata.
